title: Imaginary Barrier, Real Transfer: Non-Hermitian Dynamical Tunnelling
abstract: We identify a non-Hermitian counterpart of dynamical tunnelling induced by a localised absorbing region in a symmetric confining potential. The absorbing region, described by an imaginary potential barrier, induces an effective double-well structure with a pair of long-lived states that have little population in the barrier. In contrast to the periodic tunnel oscillations through a real barrier, the system slowly evolves towards equal population of the two sides, while the absorbing region remains only weakly populated. We demonstrate this generic mechanism in two continuous potentials, and capture its essence analytically in a minimal $3\times 3$ matrix model. We propose a realistic optical waveguide setup for the experimental observation of the effect.
summary: This paper explores non-Hermitian dynamical tunnelling caused by localized absorbing regions within a confining potential. It shows that this process leads to a slow relaxation towards equal population on both sides, contrasting sharply with the periodic oscillations seen in standard quantum tunneling. The findings are demonstrated using analytical models and proposed for experimental observation in optical waveguides.
main_problem: The paper investigates non-Hermitian dynamical tunnelling, which is the counterpart of standard quantum tunneling when the potential barrier is absorptive (imaginary) rather than real.
main_result: Instead of periodic oscillations seen with a real barrier, the system slowly relaxes towards an equal population on both sides separated by the imaginary absorbing region.
method: The analysis uses numerical propagation methods for continuous potentials and derives an effective $3 	imes 3$ matrix model to capture the core physics analytically.
model_or_system: The models include a particle in a harmonic trap with Gaussian absorption, or an infinite square well with a rectangular imaginary barrier. The phenomenon is also mapped onto coupled waveguides for experimental realization.
key_observables: Population distribution over time (relaxation to equal population), eigenvalues/eigenvectors of the effective Hamiltonian, and spatial intensity profiles in optical waveguides.
important_parameters: Absorption strength ($\Gamma G$ or $\Gamma_0$), coupling constant ($v$), and waveguide parameters like wavelength ($\lambda$) and refractive index $n(x)$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes natural units ($\hbar=m=\omega=1$) for the initial models, and the overall probability decay is noted due to the finite nature of the absorbing barrier.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate potential profiles and eigenvalue spectra vs. absorption strength; time evolution snapshots show relaxation to equal population in two halves of a trap or waveguide structure.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from analyzing simple continuous potentials (harmonic/infinite well) to deriving an effective $3 	imes 3$ matrix model, culminating in the proposal and simulation of an experimental setup using optical waveguides.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant for AMO physics and quantum optics as it deals with open quantum systems dynamics, engineered dissipation, and non-Hermitian Hamiltonians, which are key areas in modern photonics and cavity QED.

Top row: left: Real confining potential V (x) (solid grey) and imaginary barrier Γ(x) (dashed magenta), for ΓG = 10 and σ = 0.1; middle and right: real parts Re(E) (middle) and imaginary parts Im(E) (right) of the nine complex eigenvalues with the lowest real parts as functions of the peak absorption strength ΓG, symmetric modes are plotted in blue, antisymmetric ones in red. Bottom row: Probability distributions in the two eigenstates with the lowest real part of the energy (even in blue, odd in red) depicted within the potential (dashed grey) for different values of ΓG, from left to right: ΓG = 1, 8, 10, 20.

FIG. 2. Non-Hermitian tunnelling in a harmonic trap with a central Gaussian imaginary barrier. Snapshots of the (nor- malised) probability distribution plotted at the height of the expected value of the real energy in the external potential for σ = 0.1 and ΓG = 20 for three different times (t = 0 (top left), t = 5 (top right), and t = 100 (bottom left)); bottom right: time evolution of the probability in the right (green) and left (orange) half of the potential and total norm (dashed black).

FIG. 3. Non-Hermitian tunnelling in a box of size 2L = 8 with a central rectangular imaginary barrier of width 2a = 2. Top: Real (left) and imaginary (right) parts of eigenvalues as functions of Γ0, dashed black lines indicate the asymptotic eigenvalues for large Γ0; bottom left: Equal superposition of the doublet states, localised in the right half of the effective double well for Γ0 = 3. The box boundaries are indicated by grey lines, and the absorption profile by a dashed magenta line; bottom right: time evolution of the probability in the right (green) and left (orange) wells, and in the absorbing region (purple), and total norm (dashed black).

FIG. 4. Real (left) and imaginary (right) parts of the eigen- values of the minimal matrix model as functions of the loss parameter γ, for unit coupling v = 1. The energies of the two symmetric states are displayed as dashed blue lines, that of the antisymmetric state as solid red line.
